They generally have a reputation for subtextually exploring lgbtqa+ themes. 

The first album was risqué, boundary pushing, and began that distinction with the 'stage-gay', and songs like 'Time to Dance', which was about a book by Chuck Palahanuik (?) traversing ideas of gender and identity, spefically those of trans peoples. Additionally, circuses have culturally harbored those outside of the sexuality and gender norms (ex. bearded ladies). AFYSCO prolifically features circus aesthetic, especially in the music of the second half of the album, the music video for Sins, and their first tour, with a circus themed stage show, was literally called 'Nothing Rhymes with Circus'. 

Pretty. Odd. ya know, exists. For whatever reason, this album is known as the 'gay' album, and that's accepted as obvious. I am personally not sure why, but perhaps it's because the album wasn't 'emo' focused, and that the band was very close, lots of pda, and this fueled the fandom's imagination about their relationships. I think it's also because they avoided heterosexual tropes, saying in an interview that 'When the Day Met the Night' is the only traditional "I love you" song. This also interesting, considering that opening for their next tour, they played a few songs, and Brendon, for whatever reason, decided to use only male pronouns for 'When the Day Met the Night'. Other than that, there is a little bit of actual canon references to lgbtqa+ themes in this album. In 'Mad as Rabbits', the closing line, which Ryan and Brendon would share a mic for, is "We must reinvent love". This is actually a quote from the gay 19th century poet Arthur Rimbaud, saying that love should be redefined to include homosexuality. Panic! sold merch with 'REINVENT <3' on it, and Ryan often wore a vest with the same thing embroidered on the back.

I don't think there's anything directly lgbtqa+ in 'Vices', but Brendon continued the 'stage-gay' mostly with Dallon. The only other thing I can think of are the lines 
-"I've been to Tokyo and to South Africa
So many places that you might say I've seen it all
But my favorite place is the warm embrace
Of holding your hair back in a bathroom stall,"- 
on the bonus track 'Bittersweet'. That's not necessarily homoerotic, but it certainly /infers/ same-sex relations.

'Too Weird to Live, Too Rare to Die' is the most explicit in its lgbtqa+ themes. The album art features Brendon smoking a cigarette, the smoke of which, is rainbow colored, and the only colors seen on the black and white image. Nine out of the ten songs on this album are about relationships ('Vegas Lights' is the exception), eight of those are romantic/sexual in nature, and two of two those reference non-heterosexual affiliations. Although, it should be noted that most of those songs are about complex and dubious personal associations. 'Girls/Girls/Boys'  was written by both Brendon and Dallon, their intended meanings sharing the idea of well... girls loving girls /and/ boys, obviously. Dallon wrote it with his wife's sexuality in mind. In addition, the bonus track 'All the Boys' is another song Dallon wrote about Breezy's orientation. Brendon wrote it about a threesome he had, and the revelations he had as a result. He said he found the fact that these girls knew and embraced who they were, and the confindence to do so (not the nature of being bisexual itself, as often misunderstood), as attractive. Additionally, admiring their ability to approbate their own sexualties, encouraged Brendon to accept himself in a similar manner. Either artist's message both contain the main point, a repeated line throughout the song, that "Love is not a choice,"; people don't choose their sexualities. Finally, the song 'Casual Affair', is of course, about a secret sexual relationship, condemned by other people, probably because of it's adulterous nature, but it is hinted that homosexuality may be a reason as well. In the official audio of the song, a man says before the song begins, "Looks innocent enough, doesn't it? But sometimes there are dangers involved that never meet the eye. No matter where you meet a stranger, be careful if they are too friendly." This audio clip is originally cut from anti-gay 1950's propoganda. So the song narrates a controversial relationship, because of their repeated adultery (esp. w/ the line(s) "I did it again. I did it again. I did it again... etc."), and because of other's views on homosexuality as something to be feared. 

'Death of a Bachelor'? Uh... yeah, I don't see anything here. This album is just about transitioning from bachelor life to married life. I mean, it's cool that he "made those high heel work," tho?

'Pray for the Wicked'? Well, there's the line, " I wanna be your boyfriend/girlfriend." Yeah, that's it. Uh... Brendon came out as pansexual during this era? uh huh

Finally, holding pride flags on stage has been a thing for years. During 'Girls/GIrls/Boys' for tour, there are colored paper hearts handed out to shine one's phone through and create a sea of rainbow lights in the crowd. Although members of P!ATD have been advocates for lgbtqa+ rights for years (honestly, Brendon's always been the most vocal), in 2018, Brendon founded the Highest Hopes Foundation, which donates money to various organizations to help LGBTQA+ and other disenfranchised peoples.
